source_text: Iam vero quis risum teneat prudentium, cum ad haec quae subdidisti exempla pervenerit? Ais enim: De ipsis verbis Apostoli refutaretur, non religiosae voluntatis, sed libidinosae voluptatis pudens nominator et impudens praedicator. De ipsis quippe seminibus, quae in agris agricolae seminant, potest iste redargui. Cur enim non credamus Deum potuisse in paradiso concedere homini beato de suo semine, quod concessum videmus agricolis de tritici semine; ut eo modo illud sereretur, sicut hoc seritur, sine ulla pudenda libidine? [n32] . Quam venuste pudens nominator et impudens praedicator dat omnino incompositos motos, et circulatorum carmina dicit. Sed illud aliud nisi laetissime legi non potest; quoniam si non peccasset Adam, sic potuit mulier, sicut seges, ad fecunditatem parari; forte ut per omnes articulos ac per minutas corporum fistulas, quas medici povrou" vocant, spicae erumperent filiorum; atque ita omnibus laeta partibus, partus pro pediculis exsudaret. Sed si aliqui et per oculos erumperent, auferrentur lumina parienti, et si pupularum globulis examina galeata prodirent, imprecaretur sine dubio caecitas orbitatem. Nec difficulter sane, non parta, sed sudata soboles necaretur, atque haberetur gens, ut apud fabulas Myrmidonum, ita apud Manichaei dogmata, vel pedicularia, vel publicaria. Sed haec esset fetura mulieris; vir autem quid posset efficere? Admoveret nimirum non membra, sed ferramenta, et genitalium vacuus imprimeret vomeres ac ligones. Grates ergo et amplissimae primorum hominum debentur errori, quo tam beatae naturae tormenta vitata sunt. Mitius partus agit cum feminis, et maritus, quam si aut aratra sentirent, aut importuna per totum corpus fecunditate silvescerent. Impleantur Manichaeorum facies ignominia, et quaerant nomen tuum, Domine. O portenta criminantium innocentes et Deum, suffragia argumentorum et testimoniorum! Cur, inquit, non credamus quia potuit aliter fieri na tura, quam facta conspicitur? Quasi quaeratur quid potuerit, et non quid instituerit Deus. Si libet ea libidine opinandi quae sunt facta reprehendere, ut dicamus, quia fieri aliter potuerunt, ideo quae sunt instituta non reddunt naturae bonae testimonium; pronuntiemus quia potuit Deus bicipites facere mortales, ideo unicipites, et qui pedibus insisterent male sunt facti; fieri enim capitati ab utraque parte potuerunt; quae forma in quibusdam solet apparere vermiculis, quorum alvum vertex ambifariam natus includit, ut ab utroque incipientes ex humero, finem habere intellegantur in medio. Admittantur ista ludibria, et quis erit delirandi finis? Potuit ergo facere Deus, ut de terra cum floribus homines germinarent; quantum ad virtutem, potuisse non abnuo; sed noluit nisi ut de sexibus nascerentur. Nunc ergo quaeritur quid fecerit, non quid potuerit. In quo loco furiosa responsio est, ut dicatur: Malum est quod est, quia potuit Deus aliter facere; hoc est enim laudare Deum in vituperationem sui, et in maculam consilii eius omnipotentiam praedicare. Non solum nulla laudatio, verum etiam ingens contumelia est, dare viribus quod sapientiae detraxeris, et dicere adfuisse Deo fortitudinem, sed defuisse consilium. Pertingit omnino ad negationem potentiae, reprehensio consulentiae; non omnia potest, si ordinare bene non potest. Immo si sapientiae sublimitate deficitur, nihil de reverentia divinitatis retentat; quod quia suspicari profanissimum est, recurrit illud, quo tradux vestra iugulatur. Deus qui fecit omnia bona valde, nihil ita instituit, ut in illo genere quod factum est, fieri potuisse aut aptius, aut rationabilius, approbetur. Sapientia quippe et omnipotentia ex aequo praeditus non institueret, quod homunculus posset iure reprehendere. Quaecumque ergo in omnibus omnino creaturis naturalia docentur, ita summe facta sunt, ut affectata in his emendatio, stulta et profana doceatur. Ut ergo forma equi, forma bovis habent quidem in mutua collatione distantiam, in suis tamen generibus aptam ex omni parte concinentiam ita sortitae sunt, ut nec debuerit, nec potuerit aut equus aut bos, secus quam formatus videtur, institui (qua regula licet omnia natantia, repentia, gradientia, volitantia, postremo aetherea caelestiaque percurrere; nullius forma quippe melius, quam illi cui parabatur generi, institui potuisse convincitur); ita et homo quem supra iam gradientium generalitas indicavit, sic est per universa formatus, ut melius a nullo fingi posset; qui accepit prudenter in corpore et locos decoris, et locos pudoris, ut in se ipso et verecundiam et confidentiam disceret; ne et deformis videretur, si esset per cuncta velatus; et deses redderetur ac negligens, si semper esset per cuncta vulgatus. Ac per hoc fecunditas humana, non alia quam quae habet, utriusque sexus debuit membra suscipere, non aliam ratio nem viscerum, non alios sensus, non aliam voluptatem. Admoneamus igitur Manichaeos, ut desinant reprehendere divinae facta sapientiae, ut opinionum suarum corrigant pravitatem; quia nec ad quaestionem attinet, si aliter homines quam universitas testis est, generaturi fuisse dicantur; nec melius eos fieri potuisse quam facti sunt, ut ratio, ita et Scriptura testatur, quae clamat Deum non solum bona, sed etiam valde bona fecisse omnia [n33] . Ac per hoc ut per totum opus, hic quoque Manichaeorum dogma collapsum est. In futuro autem tempore gloriosiora corpora, nec opis egentia, fore beatorum fatemur. Sed et hoc ipsum optime institutum est a Deo iustissimo ac sapientissimo, ut statum praemii neutiquam natura perverteret; sed esset primus gradus, in quo consisteret ingenuitas naturalis, et de quo, pro iure arbitrii liberi, vel ad poenarum ima descenderet, vel ad gloriarum cacumen per eas vias, quas Deus instituit, niteretur.
pass_a_gloss: Now indeed who of the prudent would hold laughter, when he shall have arrived at these examples which you subjoined? For you say: From the Apostle's own words he would be refuted, not a modest namer of a religious will but a shameless preacher of a lustful pleasure. For from the seeds themselves which farmers sow in the fields this man can be redargued. For why should we not believe God could have granted in paradise to the blessed human concerning his own seed what we see granted to farmers concerning wheat seed; that in that manner it would be sown, as this is sown, without any shameful lust? How charmingly the modest namer and shameless preacher gives altogether uncomposed motions, and speaks the songs of mountebanks. But that other thing cannot be read except most gladly; because if Adam had not sinned, a woman could have been prepared for fertility like a crop; perhaps so that through all the joints and through the minute pipes of bodies, which physicians call poroi, spikes of sons would burst out; and thus happy in all parts she would sweat out births instead of lice. But if some also burst out through the eyes, lights would be taken from the one giving birth, and if helmeted swarms came forth from the globes of the pupils, blindness would without doubt curse childlessness. Nor with difficulty indeed would offspring not born but sweated be killed, and there would be a nation, as in the fables of the Myrmidons, so in Manichaeus's dogmas, either of lice or of tax-farmers. But this would be the woman's offspring; but what could the man accomplish? He would apply namely not members but tools, and empty of genitals would press ploughshares and mattocks. Thanks therefore and most ample are owed to the error of the first humans, by which the torments of so blessed a nature were avoided. Birth acts more mildly with women, and a husband, than if they either felt ploughs or grew wild with untimely fertility through the whole body. Let the faces of the Manichaeans be filled with ignominy, and let them seek your name, Lord. O portents of those accusing innocents and God, suffrages of arguments and testimonies! Why, he says, should we not believe that nature could have been made otherwise than it is seen made? As if it is asked what he could, and not what God instituted. If it pleases by that lust of opining to blame things that were made, so that we say that because they could have been made otherwise, therefore those which were instituted do not render testimony of a good nature; let us pronounce that God could have made mortals two-headed, therefore the one-headed, and those who stand on feet, were made badly; for they could have been made headed from each part; which form is accustomed to appear in certain little worms, whose belly a vertex born on both sides encloses, so that beginning from each from the shoulder they are understood to have an end in the middle. Let those mockeries be admitted, and what will be the end of raving? God therefore could have made that humans germinate from the earth with flowers; as to power, I do not deny he could have; but he was unwilling except that they be born from the sexes. Now therefore it is asked what he made, not what he could. In which place the reply is furious, that it be said: What is is evil, because God could have made otherwise; for this is to praise God into a blaming of himself, and to preach omnipotence into a stain of his counsel. It is not only no praise, but even a huge insult, to give to powers what you have drawn from wisdom, and to say that fortitude was present to God, but counsel was lacking. Blame of counsel altogether reaches to a negation of power; he cannot all things, if he cannot order well. Nay if he is deficient in sublimity of wisdom, he retains nothing of the reverence of divinity; which because it is most profane to suspect, that recurs by which your tradux is slaughtered. God who made all things very good instituted nothing so that in that kind which was made it is approved that it could have been made either more aptly or more reasonably. For endowed equally with wisdom and omnipotence he would not institute what a little human could rightly blame. Whatever therefore in all creatures altogether are taught as natural have been so supremely made that an affected emendation in them is taught foolish and profane. Therefore as the form of a horse, the form of an ox have indeed in mutual comparison a distance, yet in their own kinds they have received an apt harmony from every part, so that neither ought nor could either a horse or an ox be instituted otherwise than it is seen formed (by which rule it is allowed to run through all swimming, creeping, walking, flying, finally ethereal and heavenly things; for the form of none is convicted to have been able to be instituted better than for that kind for which it was being prepared); so also the human whom the generality of walkers already indicated above is so formed through all things that he could be fashioned better by no one; who received prudently in the body both places of becomingness and places of modesty, that in himself he might learn both reverence and confidence; lest he both seem deformed if he were veiled through all things; and be rendered idle and negligent if he were always made public through all things. And through this human fertility ought to take up no other members of each sex than it has, not another reason of viscera, not other senses, not another pleasure. Let us therefore warn the Manichaeans to cease blaming the deeds of divine wisdom, to correct the crookedness of their opinions; because it neither pertains to the question if humans are said to have been about to generate otherwise than the universe is witness; nor that they could have been made better than they were made, as reason so also Scripture testifies, which cries that God made all things not only good but even very good. And through this as through the whole work, here also the dogma of the Manichaeans has collapsed. But in a future time we confess that the bodies of the blessed will be more glorious, not needing help. But this itself also was most well instituted by a most just and most wise God, that nature would by no means pervert the status of the reward; but there would be a first step, in which natural freeborn-ness would stand, and from which, according to the right of free decision, it would either descend to the depths of punishments or strive to the peak of glories through those ways which God instituted.

pass_b_english: What wise reader could hold back laughter on reaching the examples you next added? You say: ‘The apostle’s own words would refute this man, who bashfully names and shamelessly praises not a devout will but lustful pleasure. The very seeds farmers sow in the fields can refute him. Why should we not believe that God could have granted a blessed human being in paradise, concerning his own seed, what we see granted to farmers concerning wheat seed: that the former could be sown as the latter is, without any shameful lust?’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.14.29). How charmingly this bashful namer and shameless praiser makes utterly disorderly gestures and chants the songs of street entertainers!

But the other point cannot be read without great amusement: if Adam had not sinned, a woman could have been prepared for fertility like a crop field. Perhaps ears of children would burst out through every joint and through the tiny channels of the body which doctors call pores. Fertile in every part, she would sweat offspring instead of lice. But if some burst through her eyes, the mother would lose her sight; and if helmeted swarms emerged from the little globes of her pupils, blindness would undoubtedly pray for childlessness. Offspring not born but sweated out could easily be killed. We would thus have a race, like the Myrmidons in fables, but in Manichaean doctrine a race of lice or fleas. That would be the woman’s production. What could the man do? He would of course apply tools, not organs; deprived of genitals, he would drive in plowshares and hoes. The first human beings’ fault therefore deserves the fullest thanks, because it spared such a blessed nature these torments! Childbirth and a husband treat women more gently than if they felt plows or grew wild with importunate fertility all over their bodies.

‘Let the Manichaeans’ faces be filled with disgrace, and let them seek your name, Lord’ (adapted from Psalm 83:16; LXX/Vulgate 82:17). What monstrous accusers of the innocent and God! What support from arguments and testimonies! ‘Why,’ he asks, ‘should we not believe nature could have been made differently from what we see?’ (Psalm 83:16) As though the question were what God could have done rather than what he established! If this lust for conjecture entitles us to criticize what was made—saying that because things could have been made differently, their actual arrangements do not testify to a good nature—let us declare that God could have made mortals two-headed. Therefore one-headed people who stand on their feet were badly made: they could have been given a head at each end. This shape sometimes appears in little worms, whose belly is enclosed by a head at both ends, so that they begin from either shoulder and are understood to end in the middle. Admit these absurdities, and where will delirium stop?

God, then, could have made human beings sprout from the earth with flowers. As far as his power goes, I do not deny he could. But he willed them to be born only from the sexes. We are asking what he did, not what he could do. On this point it is a mad answer to say: ‘What exists is evil because God could have done it differently.’ (adapted from Psalm 83:16) This is to praise God as an insult to himself and proclaim his almighty power as a stain upon his judgment. It is not praise at all, but a great insult, to give to his strength what you take away from his wisdom and say that God possessed power but lacked good judgment. Criticism of his judgment reaches directly into denial of his power: he cannot do everything if he cannot arrange things well. Indeed, if he falls short of supreme wisdom, he retains no claim to reverence as God. Since even to suspect this is utterly impious, we return to the point that cuts your doctrine of inherited transmission’s throat. God, who made everything very good, established nothing in such a way that it can be proved that, within the kind actually made, it could have been made more suitably or reasonably (Genesis 1:31). Equally endowed with wisdom and almighty power, he would not establish something a mere little man could rightly criticize. Whatever is shown to be natural in all creatures whatsoever was therefore made so excellently that a proposed correction of it is shown foolish and impious.

The shape of a horse and the shape of an ox differ when compared with each other. Yet within their own kinds they have received a harmony so suitable in every respect that neither horse nor ox should or could have been established differently from the form we see. This rule can be applied to everything swimming, crawling, walking, or flying, and finally to things of the upper air and heavens: no creature’s form can be proved capable of being better established for the kind for which it was prepared. So too the human being, already included above among walking creatures, is formed throughout in a way no one could improve. Wisely, the human body received both parts for display and parts for modest concealment, so that a person would learn both modesty and confidence within himself. He would look misshapen if veiled all over, but would become idle and careless if always exposed all over. Human fertility therefore should have received no organs in either sex other than those it has, no other arrangement of internal parts, no other sensations, and no other pleasure.

Let us therefore warn the Manichaeans to stop criticizing the works of divine wisdom and correct their own perverse opinions. Saying that human beings would have reproduced differently from the way universal experience attests does not concern the question. Both reason and Scripture testify that they could not have been made better than they were: Scripture proclaims that God made everything not merely good but very good (Genesis 1:31; Sirach 39:16, Latin numbering 39:21). Thus here too, as throughout the whole work, the Manichaeans’ doctrine has collapsed. We do confess that in the future the blessed will have more glorious bodies needing no assistance. But this too was excellently established by the most just and wise God: nature should not displace the condition belonging to reward. There should be a first stage in which natural freedom stands and from which, by the right of free will, a person either descends to the depths of punishment or strives toward the summit of glory by the paths God established.
